title: Concepts used to model motion
study_design: Identify parameters of motion as vectors or scalars
Apply the vector model of forces, including vector addition and components of forces, to readily observable forces including the force due to gravity, friction and normal forces

engage.heading: The shortest way isn’t always the quickest
engage.text:
Mountaineering was first popularised by the scientist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure following his visit to Mont Blanc in 1760. At 4807 m tall, Mont Blanc is one or the tallest peaks in Europe and the young scientist was determined that the mountain would be conquered. Therefore, he offered a prize for anyone who was able to ascend Mont Blanc. It would take 26 years before the prize money was claimed by an unassuming doctor and his porter.
In 1854, mountaineering took off. This was an era that would become known as the golden age of mountaineering. Predominately British climbers, with Italian, French and Swiss guides, began ascending the high peaks of the Swiss alps for no other reason than the satisfaction of getting to the top. Mountaineering involves monitoring weather conditions, hiking challenging terrain, including steep rocks, snow and ice. The shortest way to the top of the mountains is rarely the best and the first mountaineers would carefully record their winding path to the top so that others could follow. In such hostile conditions, knowing where one camp was relative to another became a matter of life and death.
The climax of the golden era of mountaineering was when a British team of mountaineers, led by Edward Whyper, first scaled the Matterhorn on 14 July 1865.

chunks.heading: Vectors and scalars
chunks.text:
In science, all quantitative measurements are either vectors or scalars. A vector is a quantity that requires both a magnitude (size) and direction. For example, if you give someone directions to a shop, you would not say it is 500 m away, you would include a direction and say it is 500 m to the north, for example. A scalar quantity only requires a magnitude; no direction is needed. For example, if someone asks you to pour 500 mL of milk to make a cake, it would not make sense to give a direction for the the 500 mL, the action of pouring has an implicit direction.
Table 7A–1 shows a list of examples of vector and scalar quantities.

chunks.heading: Vector addition
chunks.text:
When adding any vector, you must remember that only the same types of vectors can be added. For example, you can add two velocity vectors but you cannot add a velocity vector to an acceleration vector. Vectors are often represented by arrows. The direction of the arrow indicates the direction of the vector, and the length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector.
When objects are moving in one dimension, the direction of the vector can be represented by either a positive or negative sign. In Figure 7A–2, you can represent the vectors on the balls as 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and −8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, in this case the direction right is positive. It is important to note you could also represent the vectors on the balls as −5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and 8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$; in this case the direction left is positive.

chunks.heading: Vector addition in one dimension
chunks.text: When adding two or more of the same type of vector, the vectors must be added head-to-tail; the vector being added should start where the previous vector finished. The resultant vector is then drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the final vector. The order in which you add the vectors does not affect the resultant vector.

chunks.heading: Vector addition in two dimensions
chunks.text:
When an aircraft is flying through the air, the pilot must consider the direction of the wind and which way to point the nose of the plane in order to fly straight. This is one of many examples where finding the resultant vector acting on a body is needed.
The same set of principles apply when adding vectors in one dimension to adding vectors in two dimensions. This means that vectors are added head-to-tail, and the resultant vector extends from the start of the first vector drawn to the head of the last vector drawn.

chunks.heading: Friction
chunks.text:
Friction is a force that resists the relative motion of solid surfaces and fluid layers sliding against each other. The force of friction always acts parallel to the surface. There are two main types of friction: static friction and kinetic friction.
Static friction is the force that resists the initiation of movement. Static friction helps you to push off the ground and walk, and is also why cars are able to move forwards. The static friction between your foot and the road or the tyre and the road pushes in the direction of travel, producing forwards motion. If you were to try and walk on ice, you would probably slip, and if you tried to drive on ice, the wheels would just spin. This is because there is insufficient static friction to cause forward motion.
Kinetic friction resists the motion of one object moving over another. This friction always opposes the direction of relative motion. If you push a flat box over the ground, it requires effort as you need to overcome the kinetic frictional force.
Frictional forces are also present when an object moves through a fluid (liquids and gases). These kinds of frictional forces are called drag forces. The mechanism of these frictional forces is different from solid on solid frictional force.

chunks.heading: Component vectors
chunks.text:
In many cases it is useful to break up vector into their components. For example, when a projectile is launched at an angle, it is useful to determine the horizontal and vertical components of the projectile’s velocity. This is because, if air resistance is ignored, the horizontal component of the velocity will not change but the vertical velocity will be constantly changing because it is acted upon by the force of gravity throughout its flight.
Any vector can be broken up into its component vectors by forming a right-angled triangle and then using a trigonometric function to solve for the components.

chunks.heading: Solving for unknown vectors
chunks.text: There will be situations where you will be given the resultant vector and will have to solve for an unknown vector. In these situations you can determine the unknown vector by either drawing a vector diagram or determining an equation to solve the unknown vector. The unknown vector will add to the initial vector to cause a change and produce the resultant vector. A general equation to solve for an unknown vector is shown below.

worked_examples.title: Vector addition in 1D
worked_examples.question:
A person walks 200 m east and then turns around and walks 50 m west.
a Draw a vector diagram for this situation.
b Calculate how far the person is away from the origin at the end of their journey.
steps: a Let east be to the right. The 200 m east vector is draw to the right. The 50 m west vector then starts at the end (tail) of the previous vector and points to the left indicating the direction, west.
[diagram: 200 m arrow right, 50 m arrow left from its head]

b This question is asking you to find the sum of the two displacement vectors. To find this, the vectors are added head-to-tail and the resultant vector runs from the start of the first vector to the head of the final vector, as shown below.
[diagram: resultant drawn from tail of 200 m vector to head of 50 m vector]
The magnitude of the resultant vector is found by 200 – 50 = 150 m, where the positive indicated the direction east. Therefore, the final answer is 150 m to the east.

worked_examples.title: Vector addition in 2D
worked_examples.question: A boat is moving north at 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ through a lake that has a current of 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ east. Calculate the net velocity, $v$, of the boat. Ensure that you include a direction for the velocity.
steps: First, draw a vector diagram of this situation.
Rearrange Pythagoras’ theorem, $a^2 = b^2 + c^2$, to determine the magnitude of the velocity.
Determine the angle by using a trigonometric function (sin, cos or tan):
$\tan\theta = \frac{3}{10}$

Note that the angle is measured from the north and the angle moved towards the east. Hence, the angle is written as N16.7°E, which means 16.7° from the north towards the east. Therefore, the final velocity is 10.4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ N16.7°E.

worked_examples.title: Finding total displacement
worked_examples.question: A hiker walks 5 km north, then 8 km east and finally 9 km south. What is the displacement of the hiker from their starting point? Include a direction in your answer.
steps: First, draw a vector diagram of the situation.

From the diagram, you should be able to see that the north vector will partially cancel out the south vector. This will leave a right-angled triangle that has a length of 8 km one side, 4 km on the other and the hypotenuse will be the net displacement as shown below.
Rearrange Pythagoras’ theorem, $a^2 = b^2 + c^2$, to determine the magnitude of the displacement.
Determine the angle by using a trigonometric function (sin, cos or tan):
$\tan\theta = \frac{4}{8}$
$\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{4}{8}$
The displacement is 8.94 km at E26.6°S.

worked_examples.title: Finding vector components
worked_examples.question: A cannon fires a cannonball at an angle of 28° up to the horizontal at an initial velocity of 50 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the cannonball’s initial velocity.
steps: Draw the velocity vector and then apply appropriate trigonometric functions to determine the components.
horizontal component $= 50\cos 28^\circ$
vertical component $= 50\sin 28^\circ$

worked_examples.title: Change in velocity
worked_examples.question: A ball is thrown north against a wall with a velocity of 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The ball then hits the wall and rebounds at a velocity of 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ south. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the change in velocity of the ball.
steps: Let north be positive:
$\Delta v = v_{\text{final}} - v_{\text{initial}} = (-3) - (5) = -8$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$
The negative sign indicates the direction: south.
This can also be solved by drawing a vector diagram. Because 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ south is the resultant vector, it must be drawn from the tail of the first vector, as shown below.

checkins.question: List four vector quantities and four scalar quantities.
checkins.answer:
Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, impulse, torque, electrical fields, magnetic fields
Scalars: distance, speed, mass, volume, area, energy, power, temperature, time

checkins.question: What is the difference between a vector and a scalar?
checkins.answer: A vector has a magnitude and a direction, but a scalar only has a direction.

section_questions.question: Which of the following is not a vector quantity?

A 50 kg cannon ball is launched from a cannon with a velocity of 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of inclination of 30° from the horizontal. What is the horizontal component of the cannon ball’s velocity?

A light aircraft is travelling through a storm, due north, with an air speed of 52.5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ (the speed if there was no wind). A cross wind is blowing towards the east with a velocity of 15 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. This situation is shown below.
The magnitude of the net velocity of the aircraft relative to the ground is:
A ball is thrown east at a wall with a speed of 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, the ball rebounds and travels west at a speed of 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The change in velocity of the ball is:
What is the difference between a vector and a scalar? Your answer must include an example to demonstrate your point.
section_questions.answer: A vector requires both a magnitude and direction while a scalar only requires a magnitude. For example, if a hiker walks from their campsite, their exact position can be given by their displacement, which is the distance from the campsite and the angle that they travelled. The hiker’s displacement is a vector quantity; this is much different from the scalar quantity of distance that would describe only the total distance that the hiker has covered.

section_questions.question: A ball is thrown with a velocity of 18.1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ south at an angle of 15.0° to the horizontal. Calculate the magnitude of the horizontal and vertical components of the ball’s velocity.

A car is travelling along a straight road at a constant velocity of 80 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ south.
a The driver then accelerates, which increases the thrust force to 2250 N and increases the frictional force to 1750 N. What is the net force on the car, given that the net force is the sum of all of the forces acting on the body?
b The driver then approaches a pedestrian crossing and slows down to 40 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ south. What is the magnitude and direction of the change in the car’s velocity?
section_questions.answer: $\Delta v = v_{\text{final}} - v_{\text{initial}} = (40) - (80) = -40$ $\text{km h}^{-1}$; the negative sign indicates the direction, north

section_questions.question:
An aircraft is attempting to travel north towards its landing strip. The aircraft has an air speed of 42 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. While the aircraft is trying to land a 5.55 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ wind blows from the west towards the east.
a What is the final velocity of the aircraft?
b In order to fly straight, the pilot angles the aircraft into the wind. Explain how this enables the aircraft to fly straight, draw a diagram to aid your answer.
section_questions.answer: The pilot must angle into the wind so that a component of the aircraft’s velocity cancels out the wind, allowing the plane to fly straight. As shown in the diagram below, if the pilot angles 7.53° into the wind, the west component of the aircraft’s velocity will cancel the wind, which means the plane will fly straight.

section_questions.question: During the Australian Open a tennis ball is travelling west towards a player at 25 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The player strikes the tennis ball and sends the ball back east towards their opponent at 19.5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. What was the change in velocity of the tennis ball? Include a direction in your answer.
section_questions.answer: Let west be positive: $\Delta v = v_{\text{final}} - v_{\text{initial}} = -19.5 - 25 = -44.5$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$; the negative indicates the direction, east

section_questions.answer: Find the angle that the swimmer is swimming across the river by adding the two velocity vectors. $\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{0.25}{1.43} = 9.92^\circ$. Because the swimmer will travel at this angle, a triangle can be formed with the distances: $h =$ [value missing in source]. The extra distance covered is therefore [value missing in source]

section_questions.question: c Suggest a way that the swimmer could swim directly north. Justify your answer.
section_questions.answer: They could swim partially into the current. This means a component of the swimmer’s velocity could cancel out the velocity of the current. The net result of this is that the swimmer would swim directly north.

skills.heading: Using direction in an equation
skills.text:
In any question that involves a vector quantity, the direction of the vector must be considered and incorporated into your equation. Direction can be incorporated into an equation with a positive and negative sign representing different directions. This means that whenever you encounter a problem involving vectors, one of the first things you must do is determine which direction will be positive and which direction will be negative. Once you have made this decision, write it down on the page as this will allow you to keep track of the meaning of a negative or positive answer. For example:
Question
A jet plane is moving through the air with a velocity of 150 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ south when it encounters a headwind blowing 25 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ northerly (a northerly wind blows from the north towards the south). What is the velocity of the jet plane relative to the ground?
Solution
Determine which direction is positive.
positive direction = south
Add the vectors:
$v = 150 + (-25)$
$= 125$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ south
Note that the positive answer gave the direction south.
We could also let south be negative and the solution would still be the same:
$v = -150 + 25$
$= -125$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$
The negative indicates the direction: south.
